newsitem.title: UK: EMU need not be irrevocable.
newsitem.headline: EMU need not be irrevocable.

text.p: British finance minister Kenneth Clarke said on Friday that European monetary union (EMU) need not be irrevocable, although countries joining it should assume that it would be permanent.

Clarke's comments appeared to be at odds with the Maastricht Treaty, which states that the exchange rates of participating countries will be irrevocably fixed and that they will then be replaced by a single currency.

"The intention of going into monetary union would be that this is intended to be permanent in the foreseeable future -- that everybody would fix their interest rates together, that everybody would have the same currency," Clarke said on a BBC television phone-in programme.
"Once you've got into that, the idea would be that nobody would come out."
However, Clarke noted that some previous monetary unions had ultimately ended, including one in southern Europe -- an apparent reference to a "Latin" monetary union which lasted from 1865 to 1927.
"In fact, there is never a never' in politics," he said.

"We were in monetary union with the Irish Republic for about 50 years. They pulled out of that in the 1970s. So these things can be disentangled. But no-one should go into it believing it was anything other than a lasting situation."
Monetary union is due to come into effect on January 1, 1999 with the irrevocable fixing of exchange rates.

Article 109L of the Maastricht Treaty states that at the start of the final stage, heads of government will "adopt the conversion rates at which their currencies shall be irrevocably fixed and at which irrevocably fixed rate the Ecu (European currency unit) shall be substituted for these currencies."
The European Union has since decided that the new currency will be known as the euro. Euro notes and coins are due to be introduced by 2002.
German Chancellor Helmut Kohl has said European integration, of which the single currency is a central element, must be made irreversible.
Clarke, the leading Europhile in a Conservative cabinet that contains many "Eurosceptics," said the understanding had always been that a single currency would be lasting.
"Currency things have to be fairly permanent," he said.
He agreed with a caller that financial systems could change but rejected suggestions that if Britain joined a single currency, it would hand power over its economic affairs to the European Union.
"It wouldn't affect our tax, It wouldn't affect our public spending. It wouldn't stop a British chancellor giving a budget and it wouldn't damage our national sovereignty," he said.
"The idea that all our reserves get given to the Europeans, or -- as a constituent said to me the other day -- get given to the Bundesbank, that is completely untrue."
Regardless of which party won the May 1 election, the British people would ultimately have to give their approval in a referendum before the country joined a single currency.
Clarke also dismissed suggestions that the EU could extend value-added tax (VAT) or impose new taxes in Britain against the will of its government.
"I'm extremely worried about...this suspicion we're in thrall to Brussels," he said.
Eurosceptics were trying to get Britons to believe that "someone out there -- the Germans or people in Brussels -- are plotting these things against us."
"I can only tell you that is not the real world in 1997. They have no power to impose upon us VAT on anything."
